decls.name: Std.HashMap
decls.sig: Std.HashMap.{u, v} (α : Type u) (β : Type v) [BEq α] [Hashable α] : Type (max u v)
decls.type_fullnames: (α : Type u) → Type v → [BEq α] → [Hashable α] → Type (max u v)
decls.src_statement: HashMap (α : Type u) (β : Type v) [BEq α] [Hashable α]
decls.doc:
Hash maps.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `Array`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `BEq` typeclass) to compare keys and `hash` (provided by
the `Hashable` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`EquivBEq` and `LawfulHashable` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

These hash maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `Std.Data.HashMap.Raw` and
`Std.Data.HashMap.Raw.WF` unbundle the invariant from the hash map. When in doubt, prefer
`HashMap` over `HashMap.Raw`.

Dependent hash maps, in which keys may occur in their values' types, are available as
`Std.Data.DHashMap`.

capacity.

decls.doc:
Marks a hash map as linear, which is a no-op logically.

At runtime the bucket array backing the map is first made unique, copying it if the reference is not
already unique, and then marked. If the environment variable `LEAN_ABORT_ON_NONLINEAR` is set,
every non-linear use from that point on causes a panic instead of a silent copy.

To debug where the non-linearity is coming from you can set a breakpoint on `lean_internal_panic`.

decls.doc:
Inserts the given mapping into the map. If there is already a mapping for the given key, then both
key and value will be replaced.

Note: this replacement behavior is true for `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw`.
The `insert` function on `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw` behaves differently: it will return the set
unchanged if a matching key is already present.

decls.doc:
Returns `true` if there is a mapping for the given key. There is also a `Prop`-valued version
of this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.contains a = true`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for comparisons, while for hash maps, both use `==`.

decls.name: Std.HashSet
decls.sig: Std.HashSet.{u} (α : Type u) [BEq α] [Hashable α] : Type u
decls.type_fullnames: (α : Type u) → [BEq α] → [Hashable α] → Type u
decls.src_statement: HashSet (α : Type u) [BEq α] [Hashable α]
decls.doc:
Hash sets.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash set consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of keys. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash set doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `Array`. Users should make sure that the hash set is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash set uses `==` (provided by the `BEq` typeclass) to compare elements and `hash` (provided by
the `Hashable` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`EquivBEq` and `LawfulHashable` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

These hash sets contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `Std.Data.HashSet.Raw` and
`Std.Data.HashSet.Raw.WF` unbundle the invariant from the hash set. When in doubt, prefer
`HashSet` over `HashSet.Raw`.

decls.doc:
Inserts the given element into the set. If the hash set already contains an element that is
equal (with regard to `==`) to the given element, then the hash set is returned unchanged.

Note: this non-replacement behavior is true for `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw`.
The `insert` function on `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw` behaves
differently: it will overwrite an existing mapping.

decls.doc:
Checks whether an element is present in a set and inserts the element if it was not found.
If the hash set already contains an element that is equal (with regard to `==`) to the given
element, then the hash set is returned unchanged.

Equivalent to (but potentially faster than) calling `contains` followed by `insert`.

decls.type_fullnames: {α : Type u} → {x : BEq α} → {x_1 : Hashable α} → Std.HashSet α → α → Bool
decls.src_statement: contains (m : HashSet α) (a : α) : Bool
decls.doc:
Returns `true` if the given key is present in the set. There is also a `Prop`-valued version of
this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.contains a = true`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` use
`==` for comparisons, while for hash sets, both use `==`.

Checks if given key is contained and returns the key if it is, otherwise `none`.

decls.name: Std.HashSet.get
decls.sig: Std.HashSet.get.{u} {α : Type u} [BEq α] [Hashable α] (m : Std.HashSet α) (a : α) (h : a ∈ m) : α

Retrieves the key from the set that matches `a`. Ensures that such a key exists by requiring a proof
of `a ∈ m`. The result is guaranteed to be pointer equal to the key in the set.

decls.name: Std.HashSet.getD

decls.doc:
Checks if given key is contained and returns the key if it is, otherwise `fallback`.
If they key is contained the result is guaranteed to be pointer equal to the key in the set.

decls.name: Std.HashSet.get!

decls.doc:

If no panic occurs the result is guaranteed to be pointer equal to the key in the set.

decls.name: Std.HashSet.isEmpty

decls.src_statement: isEmpty (m : HashSet α) : Bool
decls.doc:
Returns `true` if the hash set contains no elements.

Note that if your `BEq` instance is not reflexive or your `Hashable` instance is not
lawful, then it is possible that this function returns `false` even though `m.contains a = false`
for all `a`.

decls.sig: Std.HashSet.insertMany.{u, v} {α : Type u} {x✝ : BEq α} {x✝¹ : Hashable α} {ρ : Type v} [ForIn Id ρ α] (m : Std.HashSet α) (l : ρ) : Std.HashSet α

decls.src_statement:
insertMany {ρ : Type v} [ForIn Id ρ α] (m : HashSet α) (l : ρ) :
    HashSet α
decls.doc:
Inserts multiple mappings into the hash set by iterating over the given collection and calling
`insert`. If the same key appears multiple times, the first occurrence takes precedence.

Note: this precedence behavior is true for `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw`. The `insertMany` function on
`HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw` behaves differently: it will prefer the last
appearance.

drop_in_notes.text: HashMap.iter/keysIter/valuesIter and HashSet.iter have no written return type; the elaborated type is `@Std.Iter σ (α × β)` where the implicit state σ is `Std.Iterators.Types.Map (Flatten (Map (ArrayIterator (Std.DHashMap.Internal.AssocList α _)) …))` built over `Std.DHashMap.Internal.AssocList.AssocListIterator`. So the elaborated statements of the 12 iterator lemmas (toList_iter, toListRev_iter, toArray_iter, *_keysIter, *_valuesIter, HashSet.*_iter) mention DHashMap bucket internals and the Iterator instances on them. A drop-in can reproduce the source statements (`m.iter.toList = m.toList`), which re-elaborate against its own state type. It cannot reproduce the elaborated terms, so user code that writes the state type out breaks. The consumers only need `[Iterator σ Id β]` for toList/toListRev/toArray. `for x in m.iter` and `Iter.toHashSet` also need IteratorLoop, and the docs promise Finite and Productive. No HashMap-specific iterator instances exist. Std gets Iterator/Finite/IteratorLoop from the generic Std.Iterators.Types.{Map, Flatten, ArrayIterator} instances plus three on Std.DHashMap.Internal.AssocList.AssocListIterator: instIteratorAssocListIteratorIdSigma, instFiniteAssocListIteratorIdSigma and instIteratorLoopAssocListIteratorIdSigmaOfMonad.
keysIter and valuesIter force `{α β : Type u}` (same universe); iter does not.

The public structure field `HashMap.inner : DHashMap α (fun _ => β)` (with its constructor `HashMap.mk`, `rec`, `mk.inj`, `mk.injEq` and `mk.sizeOf_spec`) and `Equiv.inner : m₁.inner.Equiv m₂.inner` (so `Equiv.mk` too) name DHashMap and DHashMap.Equiv. HashSet.inner is `HashMap α Unit`, and HashSet.Equiv.inner is `m₁.inner.Equiv m₂.inner`, which is HashMap.Equiv. A drop-in cannot reproduce the HashMap ones. Only code that uses `m.inner`, `m.1`, `⟨d⟩` or `⟨h⟩ : Equiv` breaks, and no lemma statement in Lemmas.lean mentions `inner`.

None of the 678 HashMap/Lemmas.lean or 320 HashSet/Lemmas.lean theorem statements mentions Std.DHashMap, Raw, Std.Internal.List or any other internal. Their non-HashMap vocabulary is core only: List (Perm, Pairwise, Nodup, findSomeRev?, attach/unattach, filter, map, foldl/foldlM, contains, …), Array, Option (pfilter, pbind, pmap, get, …), BEq/EquivBEq/LawfulHashable/LawfulBEq/ReflBEq, GetElem?/Membership/Union/Inter/SDiff/Singleton/Insert/EmptyCollection, ForIn/ForM, and `ForIn.toList` (Init.Control.Id). The only Std.Internal mention is the class `Std.Internal.PureForIn` in two instances.

The Lemmas files register `instance : Std.Internal.PureForIn m' (HashMap α β) (α × β)` and `… (HashSet α) α` (needing [Monad m'] [LawfulMonad m']). They rest on `forIn_toList : ForIn.toList c = c.toList`. PureForIn is consumed by Std.WP (the mvcgen spec lemmas for `for` loops), so a drop-in has to provide the same instance or mvcgen loses its loop specs over the map.
`LawfulGetElem (HashMap α β) α β (fun m a => a ∈ m)` lives in Lemmas.lean and requires [EquivBEq α] [LawfulHashable α]. HashSet has no GetElem instance.

Std uses `variable {_ : BEq α} {_ : Hashable α}`, so most operations and nearly all lemmas take BEq/Hashable as anonymous implicit binders (`{x✝ : BEq α}`), not instance-implicit ones. Some definitions instead take `[BEq α] [Hashable α]`: emptyWithCapacity, ofList, ofArray, unitOfList, unitOfArray, union, inter, diff, filterMap, map, iter*, HashSet.get/getD/get!. `beq` takes `{x✝ : Hashable α} … [BEq α] [BEq β]`. Binder order also varies between sections: in Union, Inter and Diff, β comes after the BEq/Hashable binders. `sig` records the exact order and kinds for `@`-explicit and named-argument use.

Lean 4.35's `cbv` evaluator is wired in. 10 definitions are `@[cbv_opaque]` (HashMap emptyWithCapacity/insert/erase/filter/filterMap/map and HashSet emptyWithCapacity/insert/erase/filter), and 58 lemmas are `@[cbv_eval]` rewrite rules (contains/get?/getElem?/getElem!/getD of emptyWithCapacity/insert/erase, insertMany_nil/cons, ofList_eq_insertMany_empty, ofArray_eq_ofList, the primed filter/filterMap lemmas, the map lemmas, getKey*_filter_key). A drop-in should carry the same attributes for `cbv` and `decide +cbv` behaviour to match.

`contains_eq_false_iff_not_mem` gets `simp` only through `attribute [simp] …` on the last line of each Lemmas file. grind_pattern commands supply e-matching patterns for size_le_size_insertMany, size_insertMany_list_le, size_ofList_le, size_filterMap_le_size and size_filter_le_size (HashMap), and for size_le_size_insertMany, size_insertMany_list_le, size_ofList_le and size_filter_le_size (HashSet).
One deprecated alias must exist for drop-in: `HashMap.union_insert_right_equiv_union_insert` → `union_insert_right_equiv_insert_union` (since 2025-11-03).

Four statements elaborate to terms that contain their own auxiliary constants: getKey_insert (`_proof_1` from `by simpa`), getElem?_insertMany_list (`match_1`), getElem_filterMap' (`_proof_1`) and keys_filter (`match_1`). These are regenerated automatically when the same source text is elaborated. They are recorded so a JSON-driven statement generator does not try to name them.

Some definitions sit in an `Unverified` section with no or almost no lemmas. HashMap: partition (0), values (2, both about empty), valuesArray (0), unitOfArray (1: unitOfArray_eq_unitOfList), ofArray (1: ofArray_eq_ofList), Internal.numBuckets (0), Repr (0) and beq (only through instBEq, 4). HashSet: partition (0), ofArray (1), Internal.numBuckets (0), Repr (0) and beq (through instBEq, 4). `Internal.numBuckets` is a public def whose value depends on the representation.

45 lemmas (28 HashMap, 17 HashSet) are propositional equalities between maps or sets themselves, not `~m`. They constrain the implementation beyond the entry-list model. (a) ofList_nil : ofList [] = ∅ (that is, emptyWithCapacity 8), ofList_singleton, ofList_cons, ofList_eq_insertMany_empty, ofArray_eq_ofList, unitOfList_* , unitOfArray_eq_unitOfList, insertMany_nil/_cons/_append/_list_singleton and insertManyIfNewUnit_nil/_cons/_list_singleton force insertMany/ofList/ofArray/unitOfList (on lists) to be literally a left fold of insert/insertIfNew starting from the given map or from ∅. Pre-reserving capacity or bulk-building would break them unless the table layout is history-independent. (b) erase_empty and erase_emptyWithCapacity: erasing from an empty map returns the identical structure. (c) containsThenInsert_snd, containsThenInsertIfNew_snd and getThenInsertIfNew?_snd: the fused operations return exactly the structure insert/insertIfNew would. (d) insert_eq_insert, singleton_eq_insert, union_eq, inter_eq, diff_eq and markLinear_eq hold by definition. The JSON lists them via `eq_type_head` ∈ {Std.HashMap, Std.HashSet}.

toList order is unspecified (insert only up to List.Perm: toList_insert_perm), but every traversal must agree with it exactly. The equalities that require this: map_fst_toList_eq_keys, toArray_toList and toList_toArray, toArray_keys and toList_keysArray, map_fst_toArray_eq_keysArray, fold_eq_foldl_toList and foldM_eq_foldlM_toList (plus the _keys, _toArray and _keysArray variants), forM_eq_forM_toList, forIn_eq_forIn_toList, any_toList and all_toList, toList_iter, toList_keysIter and toList_valuesIter_eq_toList_map_snd. values is unconstrained apart from emptiness.

The HashSet.ofList docstring says "the last element in the collection will be present", but the lemmas pin down first-occurrence-wins: ofList_eq_insertMany_empty, insertMany_cons with HashSet.insert = insertIfNew, and HashMap.unitOfList_eq_insertManyIfNewUnit_empty. The get?_ofList lemmas avoid the issue with distinctness hypotheses. A drop-in has to follow the lemmas, which are equalities.

These semantics show up in the statements. HashMap.insert replaces both the stored key and the value (getKey_insert returns the new k). insertIfNew keeps the old entry. HashSet.insert is `insertIfNew a ()`, so it keeps the old key. HashMap.insertMany and ofList: the last occurrence wins (getElem?_insertMany_list uses findSomeRev?). HashSet.insertMany: the first occurrence wins. HashSet.ofList = HashMap.unitOfList: per its docstring the last element is kept, yet the unitOfList lemmas are stated as `getKey?_unitOfList_of_mem` with `List.Pairwise`/distinctness hypotheses. union is right-biased (the entry from m₂ wins), and inter keeps the entries of m₁. Equiv is extensional equality on the entry model and is what all union/inter/diff and Equiv.* lemmas use. Decidable (m₁ ~m m₂) needs LawfulBEq α and LawfulBEq β.

The Repr instances print `Std.HashMap.ofList [...]` / `Std.HashSet.ofList [...]` as a literal string, and the docstrings of Array.groupByKey and List.groupByKey show that output. A drop-in's #eval output will differ unless it prints the same prefix.

Some Std API outside the two namespaces returns or consumes Std.HashMap/HashSet: `Array.groupByKey` and `List.groupByKey` (Std.Data.HashMap.Basic, returning Std.HashMap α (Array β) or (List β)), `Std.Iter.toHashSet`, `Std.Iter.Total.toHashSet`, `Std.IterM.toHashSet`, `Std.IterM.Total.toHashSet` and the theorem `Std.IterM.toHashSet_eq_fold` (Std.Data.Iterators.Consumers.{Set,Monadic.Set} and Lemmas). Users who switch would need SwissTable counterparts of these. The rest of Std that mentions HashMap (Std.Sat.AIG, BVDecide LRAT, Http, Async) is internal use, not API. No instance in Lean or Std outside the two namespaces mentions HashMap or HashSet (checked over all 207,958 constants of `import Lean, Std`).

Basic.lean and Lemmas.lean are `@[expose] public section`, so importers can unfold definition bodies (rfl/decide proofs through e.g. `instGetElem?Mem`, `insert_eq_insert` and `LawfulSingleton` are proved by rfl). The non-exported module-local theorems toList_inner and keys_inner (IteratorLemmas) and the private `ext` (Lemmas) are not visible and so not part of the API.
`get.congr_simp` and `getKey.congr_simp` (HashMap) and `get.congr_simp` (HashSet) are reserved congruence lemmas realised on demand by simp. A drop-in gets them for free.
`~m` is `scoped infixl:50 " ~m " => Equiv` in both Std.HashMap and Std.HashSet, so it is only available after `open Std.HashMap` / `open Std.HashSet`. The source statements use it.
